strengths: The paper connects a causal pathway analysis (counterfactual direct/indirect/spurious effects, following Plecko & Bareinboim 2022 and Pearl) to a concrete conditional independence criterion (Ŷ ⟂ B | Y) and then provides a practical differentiable penalty, giving the empirical method a principled grounding that most bias-mitigation baselines lack.

The two proposed estimators (DISCO_m and sDISCO) address a genuine practical gap: existing conditional distance correlation formulations (Wang et al., 2015) are computationally prohibitive in deep learning. The kernel-weighting scheme is clean, supports arbitrary combinations of binary/categorical/continuous target and bias variables, and has few hyperparameters.

The experimental protocol is fairly thorough: five datasets spanning confounder, collider, and mediator bias structures; five baselines with shared backbones; explicit hyperparameter grids and run budgets (Table 3), with HSCIC/CIRCE even given a larger search budget than DISCO; standard train-on-biased / test-on-unbiased evaluation.

The appendix contains substantial supporting material: full derivation of the TV decomposition, counterfactual graph proofs, Hilbert-space embedding arguments for Theorem 3, consistency arguments for both estimators, and counterfactual path analysis (Table 4) that usefully disentangles debiasing from predictive loss.

Reproducibility is addressed explicitly (codebase with configs, detailed dataset SCMs, LLM-use disclosure), and limitations of SAM under unobserved confounding are honestly discussed (Sec. 2.2), as are ethical concerns around the FairFace skin-tone proxy (App. E.1.4).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely a re-application of known machinery: the SAM is explicitly adopted from Plecko & Bareinboim (2022), and conditional-independence-based stability criteria exist in prior work (Quinzan et al., 2022; Veitch et al., 2021; Makar & D'Amour, 2022). The claimed generalization over Veitch et al. is asserted but not sharply demonstrated—the added value of the new formalism over simply imposing Ŷ ⟂ B | Y is not isolated experimentally.

Theorem 2 ('An MLE predictor that satisfies Ŷ ⟂ W,Z | Y also maximizes ctf-DE') is under-supported. The appendix proof (C.3) shows the direct effect is constant across (w, z), not that it is maximized; the claim is not true for arbitrary model classes (e.g., constant predictors satisfy the conditional independence trivially), and required assumptions on the model family/loss are not stated.

The consistency results for the practical estimators are proof sketches rather than proofs: Proposition 3/D.4 relies on informal steps (e.g., 'the centering terms cancel correctly', heuristic equalities for the globally weighted means) with no rigorous error analysis of the double kernel smoothing, and no rates or finite-sample behavior. For a paper whose main technical novelty is the estimators, this is a notable gap.

The central claim of 'efficient and scalable' is never empirically substantiated: no runtime, memory, or wall-clock comparison of DISCO_m/sDISCO against HSCIC/CIRCE/c-MMD is reported, despite the paper stating that existing conditional distance correlation is 'computationally prohibitive.'

Empirical gains are modest and the headline claim 'consistently outperform' is overstated: in Table 2, CIRCE beats both DISCO variants on Waterbirds (0.894 vs 0.867/0.863), and sDISCO (0.694) falls below HSCIC (0.708) on YaleB. No statistical significance tests or effect-size analysis accompany the comparisons, and gaps to the unbiased upper bound remain substantial on several datasets.

All benchmarks are small-scale image tasks; there is no multi-bias experiment in the main results despite 'scaling seamlessly to multi-bias scenarios' being a headline claim (the multi-bias setting appears only in the appendix-style path analysis on dSprites), and no experiments on tabular or truly large datasets.

Several presentation/notation issues reduce confidence: the proof of Proposition 1 in Appendix C.1 contains gaps and mislabeled indices (the conditional DE/IE quantities and P(w,z|y) weighting are dropped between Eq. 27 and the main-text Eq. 6), and the manuscript repeatedly cites 'Tab. 4a'/'Fig. E.8' inconsistently with actual labels.

strengths: The paper connects a causal framework (SAM, building on Plecko & Bareinboim 2022) to a practical regularizer (DISCO_m / sDISCO for conditional distance correlation), giving a coherent story from theory to implementation.

The estimators support continuous, categorical, and multivariate bias/target variables, which several baselines (GDRO, C-MMD) do not, and the methods scale to multi-bias settings, as demonstrated in the pathway analysis (Sec. 4.4).

Experiments cover five datasets with diverse bias mechanisms (confounder, collider, mediator), and the hyperparameter search budgets (Table 3) are reported transparently, including the larger budgets given to HSCIC/CIRCE, which is fair to the competitors.

Counterfactual sensitivity and counterfactual accuracy/R² analyses (Sec. 4.4, E.4) are a genuinely useful diagnostic contribution that disentangles debiasing from predictive loss, explaining e.g. why CIRCE sacrifices task signal.
A reproducibility statement, appendix proofs, explicit LLM-usage disclosure, and a candid discussion of the FairFace 'race' label are provided.
weaknesses: The theoretical novelty of Section 2 is incremental: the ctf-DE/IE/SE decomposition (Prop. 1) closely mirrors Plecko & Bareinboim (2022), and the conditional-independence criterion Ŷ ⊥ B | Y is already used empirically in prior fairness/bias work (Makar & D'Amour 2022; Veitch et al. 2021; Quinzan et al. 2022). The paper's claim of generalizing Veitch et al. is asserted but never precisely contrasted.

The consistency of sDISCO (Prop. 3 / D.4) rests only on an 'intuitive proof sketch.' The pivotal step—'global centering recovers conditional centering'—is asserted at population level without rigor, and the claim that sDISCO is a U-statistic version of DISCO_m is not established. Given that sDISCO is a headline contribution and underperforms markedly on YaleB (0.694 vs. 0.804 for DISCO_m), a proper proof is essential.

Theorem 2 ('MLE predictor satisfying Ŷ ⊥ W,Z|Y maximizes ctf-DE') is loosely stated: MLE maximizes total variation, which includes spurious effects; the maximization is presumably only within the constrained class, and the statement/proof do not make this precise.

The empirical claim of 'consistently outperforming' baselines is overstated: CIRCE beats both proposed methods on the only standard benchmark (Waterbirds: 0.894 vs. 0.867/0.863), and no statistical significance testing accompanies the comparisons, which have substantial overlap in ±std ranges.

The evaluation lacks broader standard benchmarks (e.g., CelebA, CMNIST, multi-domain domainbed tasks); four of five testbeds are custom or heavily re-engineered, limiting external validation of the superiority claim.

The method presumes the bias variables B are observed and the causal structure known—this identification requirement is a significant practical limitation in real applications, yet it receives only brief, informal treatment in Sec. 2.2 ('it is straightforward to show').

Kernel-based conditioning on Z inherits the curse of dimensionality; the paper does not analyze or empirically probe how DISCO behaves with high-dimensional or continuous bias variables beyond the low-dimensional synthetic settings.

Presentation defects: garbled estimator notation in Eq. 18, unnumbered propositions in Appendix C.2 cross-referenced as 'propositions 2 and 3' (a numbering collision with the main-text Propositions 2–3), and a broken sentence in the reproducibility statement, suggesting insufficient proofreading for a main-track submission.
The practical advantage of 'fewer hyperparameters' is modest: DISCO still requires λ, kernel bandwidth σ_Y, and m, versus 2–5 for baselines; this is a quantitative difference, not a qualitative one.

strengths: The paper is well organized and bridges two literatures cleanly: it grounds the empirical practice of independence-based bias mitigation (c-MMD, HSCIC, CIRCE) in a causal pathway analysis via the Standard Anti-Causal Model (SAM), yielding a clear conditional independence criterion (Ŷ ⊥ B | Y) with counterfactual interpretation (Thm. 1, Cor. 1).

The estimator theory is substantive: Theorem 3 establishes that conditional distance covariance vanishes iff conditional independence under strong negative type, with a reasonably rigorous proof built on Lyons (2013) Hilbert embeddings; DISCO_m and sDISCO make conditional distance correlation usable as a differentiable penalty, which is a genuine practical contribution given prior formulations were computationally prohibitive.

Experiments cover five datasets spanning confounder, collider, and mediator bias structures with both regression and classification targets, and both continuous and categorical bias variables; the comparison to five baselines is more thorough than typical, including deliberately larger hyperparameter budgets granted to HSCIC and CIRCE.

The counterfactual pathway analysis (Sec. 4.4, App. E.4) is a nice use of SAM beyond raw accuracy, disentangling debiasing from predictive accuracy and explaining why HSCIC/CIRCE underperform; the experiment with partially observed bias (sDISCO_X) directly illustrates the theory on unobserved confounding.

Reproducibility is well supported: full hyperparameter grids (Tab. 3), architecture details, data-generation SCMs, an explicit reproducibility statement, an LLM-usage disclosure, and a candid discussion of the FairFace skin-tone proxy and its problems.
weaknesses: The theoretical novelty of Section 2 is modest. SAM closely follows Plecko & Bareinboim (2022), and the conditional independence criterion Ŷ ⊥ B | Y is essentially the same condition already used empirically in the fairness/bias literature; the contribution is a reframing and justification rather than a new causal result, and the paper's framing as a 'unifying framework' overstates this.

Several proofs are incomplete or informal for the strength of the claims. The sDISCO consistency 'proof' (App. D.4) is explicitly a sketch that leans on the intuition that global centering recovers conditional double-centering in the population limit; bounding the bias from mixing reference points at finite bandwidth h is nontrivial and is not done. In App. C.2 and C.3, steps drop or interchange conditioning on (w, z) with brief justifications (e.g., 'Ŷ_{y'} ⊥ W_{y''} | Z'), which requires careful justification in twin-network counterfactual graphs; Theorem 2's claim that an MLE predictor satisfying the constraint maximizes the direct effect is stated but its proof and significance are thin (a direct effect can be maximized by a degenerate predictor, as the authors themselves note).

The empirical case for superiority is mixed rather than 'consistent'. sDISCO performs notably worse than DISCO_m on YaleB (0.694 vs. 0.804), worse on dSprites, and CIRCE beats both on Waterbirds (0.894 vs. 0.867/0.863). This variance between the two proposed estimators suggests sensitivity to estimator/bandwidth choices that the 'fewer hyperparameters, scales seamlessly' narrative does not fully acknowledge.

Evaluation leans heavily on synthetic or constructed-bias datasets; there are no standard strong baselines from the group-robustness literature beyond GDRO (e.g., IRM, JTT, self-training variants), and the model-selection protocol using an unbiased validation set is known to flatter independence-penalty methods (both for the proposed methods and baselines, but it limits external validity).

The claimed practical advantage of 'fewer hyperparameters' is partially offset by the kernel bandwidth σ_Y on the conditioning variable Y and, for DISCO_m, the reference count m; also, since the penalty conditions on the label Y, λ trades off bias removal against target information in a way the appendix counterfactual analysis shows is nontrivial, which somewhat undercuts the simplicity argument.

Minor presentation issues: Eq. 18 and the surrounding notation (dCov_DISCO hats) is garbled/ambiguous as rendered; the reference 'E.2.7 HYPERPARAMETERS' section is a stub pointing to a table; several appendix proof statements use inconsistent subscripts (e.g., ctf-DE_{y1,y0} vs. ctf-DE_{y0,y1}) that require reader care.

strengths: The paper makes a genuine and useful algorithmic contribution: the sDISCO single-shot factorization of the conditional distance correlation V-statistic (Theorem G.1) is clean, exactly proven, and reduces memory from O(n^3) to O(n^2), which the runtime/memory analysis in Appendix H.5 credibly demonstrates (sDISCO matches the fastest baselines at large batch sizes where naive DISCO and several baselines OOM).

The causal framing (SAM) is thoughtfully constructed: it unifies confounder, collider, and mediator bias mechanisms in anti-causal prediction and derives an observational conditional independence criterion (Ŷ ⊥ B | Y) for causal stability, connecting counterfactual path-specific analysis (Plecko & Bareinboim) to practical regularization.

Empirical evaluation is broad and reasonably rigorous: six datasets spanning regression/classification, binary/categorical/continuous biases, seven baselines including modern conditional-dependence methods (CIRCE, HSCIC, c-MMD), documented hyperparameter grids (Table 5), and a controlled counterfactual pathway analysis on dSprites with true interventions (Tables 3, 6), which is a nice demonstration beyond standard unbiased-test-set metrics.

The assumptions are explicitly analyzed (positivity/overlap, selective mediation, unobserved confounding and proxies in Section 2.2), and the limitations section is honest about the informed-bias-mitigation requirement.

The appendix transparently documents that the sDISCO implementation previously contained an error, reports the old results in Table 4, and states the corrected implementation now matches the proven factorization — an ethically commendable level of transparency.
Ethical treatment of the FairFace experiment (relabelling 'race' as 'skin tone', distinguishing labeled sex from gender) is careful and appropriate.
weaknesses: The history of the sDISCO implementation error materially weakens confidence in the empirical claims: the old (erroneous) results in Table 4 show sDISCO notably weaker (e.g., 0.619 vs. 0.687 R² on dSprites; 0.694 vs. 0.770 BAcc on YaleB), meaning the favorable comparison against CIRCE/HSCIC hinges entirely on the corrected implementation. While the correction is documented, independent verification is essential, and the code link in the abstract is empty ('Source Code:'), harming reproducibility.

Appendix A appears to be a rebuttal-style addition rather than integrated manuscript text: it contains an incomplete sentence ('Following the constructive feedback from regarding...') and is placed oddly before the technical appendices, indicating the manuscript was not carefully assembled.

The theoretical contribution of SAM/Theorems 2.3–2.4 is relatively incremental: the TV-decomposition and the sufficiency of conditional independence for blocking spurious/indirect effects largely repackage known results from Plecko & Bareinboim (2022), Veitch et al. (2021), and Makar & D'Amour (2023); the novelty is the specific framing rather than substantially new theory.

The core method requires fully observed bias variables B during training and ground-truth Y for the conditioning set; the authors acknowledge this, but it restricts applicability to the informed bias-mitigation regime and makes the practical advantage over GDRO-type group methods less clear-cut.

The consistency result for DISCO_m (Prop. F.8) relies on asymptotic bandwidth conditions (h → 0, n h^d → ∞) that are not satisfied by the fixed-bandwidth minibatch estimator actually used in training, so the theory-practice gap is not fully bridged; the local estimator consistency is largely deferred to Wang et al. (2015).

Empirical gains over the strongest baselines (GDRO, CIRCE) are modest and dataset-dependent (e.g., CIRCE beats both DISCO variants on Waterbirds; GDRO is comparable on MNLI), and some baselines are only evaluated on a subset of datasets, which slightly weakens the 'consistently outperform' claim.

Presentation has noticeable language issues throughout ('there converse', 'an candidate', 'make models to latch on', 'a defacto standard'), which, while minor, add to the impression of insufficient polish.

strengths: The paper is transparent about a serious issue: Appendix A openly discloses that the original sDISCO implementation contained an error, reports the old (flawed) results in Table 4 alongside the corrected ones, and details LLM usage. This level of disclosure is commendable.

The causal framing (SAM, TV decomposition into ctf-stable/indirect/spurious effects, Theorem 2.3 linking conditional independence to causal stability) is clearly laid out, with proofs provided in the appendix and honest discussion of assumption violations (positivity, unobserved confounding, selective mediation).

The sDISCO factorization (Theorem G.1) achieving exact O(n²) memory evaluation of the conditional distance correlation V-statistic is a neat, verifiable piece of linear algebra, with runtime/memory benchmarks (Table 7) supporting the scalability claims.

The experimental protocol is comparatively rigorous: baselines were given larger hyperparameter search grids than the proposed methods (Table 5), the counterfactual pathway analysis on dSprites (Tables 3, 6) goes beyond standard balanced-test-set evaluation, and limitations (including the requirement of observed bias labels) are discussed candidly, including a thoughtful ethical treatment of the FairFace 'race' label reinterpretation.
weaknesses: The manuscript is visibly unfinished. The abstract ends with 'Source Code:' followed by nothing, and Appendix A contains the dangling sentence 'Following the constructive feedback from [blank] regarding...' with a missing referent. For a main-track submission these are significant presentation defects that suggest inadequate final proofreading.

The headline claim that DISCO variants 'consistently outperform or are competitive' overstates the evidence. In Table 2, sDISCO is best only on MNLI (0.760 vs. GDRO 0.755, within one standard deviation), CIRCE clearly wins on Waterbirds (0.894 vs. 0.874), and several margins (e.g., DISCOm 0.860 vs. adversarial 0.846 on FairFace) are small relative to run-to-run variability. The results support 'competitive on some benchmarks', not consistent superiority.

The theoretical contribution is largely incremental. The conditional independence criterion, counterfactual effect decomposition, and conditional distance correlation are all adapted from Plecko & Bareinboim (2022), Wang et al. (2015), and Lyons (2013); the new results assemble these pieces rather than introducing substantially new theory, and the claim that the criterion is the 'best achievable approximation' under unobserved confounding is argued informally rather than proven.

There is a gap between the theory and the practice that is not fully addressed: Theorem 2.3 guarantees causal stability only under exact conditional independence, but the method enforces it via a soft penalty λ·sDISCO(Ŷ, B | Y) with a kernel bandwidth hyperparameter. No analysis is given of how far the empirical penalty must be driven to inherit the counterfactual guarantees, and sensitivity to σ_Y and λ is not reported.

The corrected-sDISCO history weakens confidence in the reported numbers: the main-text results are systematically better than the erroneous-implementation results (e.g., YaleB 0.770 vs. 0.694, MNLI 0.760 vs. 0.730), and the appendix asserts the corrected version 'inherently yields stronger empirical performance' without explaining why an exact-factorization fix (which computes the same mathematical quantity) would change performance at all, since the erroneous implementation should have been optimizing a different objective by accident.

The most impressive evidence (true counterfactual stability, Tables 3 and 6) comes only from fully controlled synthetic dSprites simulations; on the realistic datasets (Waterbirds, FairFace, MNLI), the causal claims reduce to improvements on bias-balanced test metrics, which prior work has argued are imperfect proxies for causal stability.

strengths: The paper offers a coherent two-part contribution: (1) the Standard Anti-Causal Model (SAM), which unifies confounder, collider, and mediator bias in an anti-causal prediction setting and yields the observational criterion Ŷ ⊥ B | Y as a sufficient condition for causal stability; and (2) two practical estimators (DISCO_m and sDISCO) of conditional distance correlation that make conditional-independence regularization feasible for deep networks.

The theoretical development is careful. The TV-decomposition (Prop. 2.1), the sufficiency proofs via twin/counterfactual graphs (Appendix E), and the conditional distance covariance characterization via strong negative type and Hilbert embeddings (Appendix F) are well-constructed and follow recognized machinery (Plecko & Bareinboim 2022; Lyons 2013).

The sDISCO algebraic factorization (Theorem G.1) is a genuinely useful algorithmic contribution: it computes the exact global V-statistic in O(n^2) memory instead of O(n^3), and the runtime analysis (Table 7) confirms it scales to batch sizes where both the naive estimator and several baselines OOM.

The empirical evaluation is broad: six datasets spanning vision and NLP, regression and classification, binary/categorical/continuous bias attributes, multi-bias scenarios, seven baselines with documented hyperparameter grids, and a controlled counterfactual path analysis (Tables 3, 6) that goes beyond standard unbiased-test-set reporting.

The limitations section is honest and specific (positivity requirement, informed-bias-mitigation regime, residual leakage under unobserved confounding), and the ethical discussion of the FairFace 'race'→'skin tone' reinterpretation is thoughtful rather than perfunctory.
weaknesses: The manuscript contains leftover revision artifacts that undermine presentation quality: the abstract's 'Source Code:' link is empty, and Appendix A includes text evidently responding to unnamed reviewers ('Following the constructive feedback from [blank]...'), including a confession that the original sDISCO implementation contained errors. This is transparency, but it also means the central algorithmic results changed substantially between versions (e.g., sDISCO on YaleB: 0.694 → 0.770; dSprites: 0.619 → 0.687), which weakens confidence in the reported numbers and in the validation practices around the implementation.

Novelty is more integrative than fundamental. The conditional independence criterion Ŷ ⊥ B | Y largely restates separation/risk-invariance results (Makar & D'Amour 2023; Veitch et al. 2021), SAM is a direct adaptation of Plecko & Bareinboim's path-specific fairness framework, and the estimators are computational refinements of Wang et al. (2015). The value is in the bridge to deep learning practice, not new theory.

The margin over the strongest baselines is modest and inconsistent: CIRCE beats both DISCO variants on Waterbirds (0.894 vs 0.867/0.874), and GDRO matches or exceeds sDISCO on FairFace and MNLI. Claims of 'consistently outperform' in the abstract slightly overstate Table 2.

Several proof steps are asserted rather than fully established: the consistency argument for DISCO_m (Prop. F.8) leans on 'as established by Wang et al. (2015)' for the key local convergence step, and the ratio/variance-normalization consistency under finite samples is not analyzed; the variance denominators can be near zero, and the 0/0 := 0 convention's effect on optimization is unexplored.

The framework requires observed, labeled bias variables B and correct specification of which mediators are 'unstable' (W_stable). For multi-variable bias settings the practical burden of identifying and annotating all bias attributes is acknowledged but its sensitivity to misspecification is not experimentally probed.

The kernel bandwidth σ over the conditioning variable Y and λ remain sensitive hyperparameters; the paper's claim of 'fewer hyperparameters' holds relative to HSCIC/CIRCE but the grid in Table 5 (36 runs) is comparable to adversarial training.
